concepts.term: Sound wave travelling through a solid
concepts.def: A sound wave can travel through a solid, not only through air. As it passes, it causes vibrations in the solid itself: the particles of the solid are made to vibrate about their fixed positions and pass the disturbance on to their neighbours, so the wave is carried through the material.
A thin solid membrane inside the ear. A sound wave arriving at the ear drum makes it vibrate, so the ear drum is the point at which a sound wave in air is converted into vibrations of a solid.

Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, and it is this vibration that causes the sensation of sound. If the vibration is not produced, there is no sensation of sound.

The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works only over a limited frequency range: the solid parts involved can be made to vibrate by some frequencies but not by others. Outside that range the wave disturbance is not converted into vibration of the solid.

Because the ear drum and other parts of the ear only convert sound to vibration over a limited frequency range, human hearing has both an upper and a lower frequency limit. The range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), the number of waves passing a point each second. One kilohertz (1 kHz) is 1000 Hz, so the upper limit of normal human hearing, 20 kHz, is the same as 20 000 Hz.

concepts.term: Converting sound waves into vibrations of a solid
concepts.def: A process in which a sound wave in air arrives at a solid and makes that solid vibrate. Examples: sound waves striking the ear drum and making it vibrate; sound waves striking the diaphragm of a microphone and making it vibrate.

concepts.term: Converting vibrations of a solid into sound waves
concepts.def: The reverse process, in which a vibrating solid disturbs the air next to it and sends out a sound wave. Examples: the cone of a loudspeaker vibrating and producing sound waves in the air; a struck solid object vibrating and producing a sound.

mcqs.q: A sound wave from a loudspeaker passes through a brick wall and is heard in the next room. What happens inside the wall as the sound passes through it?
options: The wave travels through tiny air gaps between the brick particles
The particles of the brick vibrate, passing the wave through the solid
The wave stops at the wall because sound can only travel in air
The wave is reflected at the surface, so only a faint echo gets through
mcqs.explain: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid: each particle vibrates about its position and passes the disturbance on.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes how sound waves cause the sensation of sound in the ear?
options: Nerves in the ear respond to the wave without anything vibrating
Sound waves make the ear drum and other parts of the ear vibrate
The ear drum only vibrates when a sound is loud enough to hear
The air inside the ear vibrates but the ear drum itself stays still
mcqs.explain: This is the process the specification states: within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, which causes the sensation of sound.

mcqs.q: The cone of a loudspeaker is made to move in and out rapidly and a sound is heard. Which conversion is taking place at the cone?
options: Sound waves in the air are converted into vibrations of a solid
Sound waves are converted into electrical signals inside the cone
The cone changes the frequency of the sound waves in the air
Vibrations of a solid are converted into sound waves in the air
mcqs.explain: The vibrating cone is a solid that disturbs the air next to it, sending out a sound wave - the solid-to-sound direction of the conversion.

mcqs.q: A microphone contains a thin diaphragm. A student speaks into the microphone. What happens at the diaphragm first?
options: The diaphragm vibrates first and then creates sound waves
The sound wave passes through gaps in the diaphragm
Sound waves in the air make the solid diaphragm vibrate
The sound is turned into electricity without anything moving
mcqs.explain: This is the same conversion as at the ear drum: a sound wave arrives at a solid and sets it vibrating.

mcqs.q: A signal generator and loudspeaker produce a sound at 30 kHz at very high volume. A student with normal hearing hears nothing. Why?
options: The conversion of the wave into vibrations does not work at that frequency
The sound is not loud enough for the ear drum to be able to vibrate at all
At 30 kHz the loudspeaker is not producing a sound wave at all
The ear drum vibrates normally but the brain ignores the signal
mcqs.explain: The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works only over a limited frequency range; 30 kHz is above 20 kHz, so the ear's solid parts are not set vibrating.

mcqs.q: The range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Written in hertz, what is the upper limit of this range?
Which one of these frequencies lies outside the range of normal human hearing?
options: 15 Hz
300 Hz
mcqs.explain: 15 Hz is below the lower limit of 20 Hz, so it lies outside the range of normal human hearing.

mcqs.q: One student taps the far end of a long metal railing. Another student, with an ear against the railing, hears the tap clearly. Which statement explains this?
options: Sound cannot travel in metal at all, so it must have come through the air
The tap sets the metal vibrating and the vibrations travel along it
The sound travels through gaps in the metal without moving it
The metal makes the sound louder so it can be heard much further
mcqs.explain: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid, so the railing itself carries the disturbance to the listener.

mcqs.q: Why does the conversion of sound waves into vibrations of solids only work over a limited frequency range?
options: Only sounds above a certain loudness can make any solid vibrate
Sound waves only exist over a limited range of frequencies
Solid parts such as the ear drum will only vibrate over a limited range
The brain, not the ear, decides which frequencies are converted
mcqs.explain: The solid can be set vibrating by some frequencies and not by others, so outside that range no conversion takes place.

mcqs.q: The ear drum and other parts of the ear can be made to vibrate only within a limited range of frequencies. What does this fact explain?
options: Why very quiet sounds cannot be heard at any frequency
Why sounds outside human hearing are not really waves
Why hearing has an upper limit but no lower limit at all
Why human hearing has an upper and a lower frequency limit
mcqs.explain: The restricted conversion sets both ends of the range of normal human hearing, 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
